title: Professional cakes: sponges, layers and heat-proof finishes

say: Professional cakes: sponges, layers, and finishes that survive the heat.
This is the video for module two of Advanced Baking and Pastry.
This module moves you from one-tin cakes to the layered, finished cakes customers pay premium prices for. First, the creaming method.

say: A Victoria sponge is equal weights of egg, butter, caster sugar and self-raising flour. Weigh the eggs you have, and match them. For example, Amaka's 7 eggs weighed 378 grams, so she used 378 grams of each.

panel.heading: Equal weights, then cream properly
items: Weigh eggs; same weight of butter, sugar, flour
Cream butter and sugar until pale, fluffy
Add egg a little at a time
Fold in flour, stop when none shows
Weigh batter into tins, bake at 180

say: Cream the butter and sugar for about 3 to 5 minutes with a mixer, until pale, almost white and fluffy. You are cutting tiny air pockets that become your rise. This is the step most people rush.

say: Whisked sponges rise mainly on egg foam. For genoise, warm the eggs and sugar over simmering water to about 40 to 45 degrees, then whisk for 8 to 10 minutes until a ribbon holds on the surface. It slices into clean thin layers, brushed with syrup.
Chiffon folds an oil and yolk batter into a firm, glossy meringue. Use a grease-free bowl and an ungreased tin, and cool it upside down, or it shrinks and sinks.
Because it uses oil, chiffon stays soft in the fridge, which suits fresh cream cakes.
For example, Blessing in Abuja is making a three-layer 20 centimetre cake. Never assemble a warm cake. Chill the layers for at least an hour, or overnight.

panel.heading: Assemble in this order
items: Cool, wrap and chill the layers
Level and split with a serrated knife
Brush each layer with syrup
Pipe a buttercream dam, then fill
Thin crumb coat, chill, final coat

say: Cut off the dome with a long serrated knife while turning the cake, and use toothpicks to mark where to split.

say: Brush each layer with simple syrup, equal weights of sugar and water. Blessing uses about 45 millilitres per layer. Too much makes a soggy cake.

say: A buttercream that is perfect in an air-conditioned room may slide in a hall at 32 degrees. American buttercream is quick and sweet: 1 part butter to 2 parts icing sugar.

panel.heading: Choose a finish for the heat
items: American buttercream: 1 butter to 2 sugar
SMBC: 1 white, 2 sugar, 3 butter
Ganache drip: 1 to 1
Firm dark ganache: 2 to 1

say: Swiss meringue buttercream is silky and less sweet. For example, 100 grams of whites, 200 of sugar and 300 of butter.

say: For Swiss meringue buttercream, heat the whites and sugar until they reach 71 degrees on a probe thermometer. This reduces the risk from bacteria such as Salmonella.

cards.d: Heat whites and sugar to 71 C on a probe thermometer before whipping. It reduces risk from bacteria.

say: Fresh cream, custards, curds, cream cheese icing and fresh fruit fillings are perishable. Keep those cakes refrigerated, and tell the customer to keep them cold.

say: Do not leave perishable food at room temperature for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is very hot. Wash hands, tools and boards, and keep raw eggs away from finished cakes.

say: To remember. Use equal weights and cream until pale. Add egg gradually. Choose genoise for structure and chiffon for chilled cakes.
Assemble cold, with a dam and a crumb coat. And pick your finish for the venue's heat, not only the photo.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Equal weights, and cream until pale
Add egg gradually; flour rescues curdling
Genoise for structure, chiffon for the fridge
Chill, dam, crumb coat, chill again
Firm ganache for hot venues
